description: Periocular phenotype: eye globe, eyelid morphology, palpebral fissure metrics, epicanthic fold, brow ridge, eyebrow morphology, and tear-trough region. Absorbs the original Eyelids and Eye Color atlas categories per the granularity decision (eye color is a single dimension, eyelid morphology is tightly coupled to eye morphology, brow region is the soft-tissue continuation of orbital anatomy). Dimensions are drawn from craniofacial anthropometry (Farkas), oculoplastic surgery (Putterman, McCord), Asian-eyelid-surgery classification literature (McCurdy, Liu, Chen), and dermatology / aging-face literature for the brow and tear-trough dimensions.

reliability_studies.method: test-retest: the identical prompt re-read against stored codings, same model, no human rater
reliability_studies.measures: reproducibility, NOT validity. Agreement between two readings says the instrument is stable, not that it is correct.
reliability_studies.corpus: publicly documented portraits of notable people, 39 ethnic groups, single frontal or three-quarter images
reliability_studies.statistic: percent agreement and Cohen's kappa over portraits where both readings gave a non-decline value
reliability_studies.decline_handling: A value meaning "could not assess" (unclear, not_visible, not_assessable, obscured, covered_unclear, not_applicable_or_*) is treated as a decline, not an answer. Scoring declines as answers makes a dimension that is never visible look perfectly reliable.
limitations: One model, one corpus, one re-read. No human inter-rater study exists for this vocabulary.

Kappa is fragile wherever one value dominates. Measured on this corpus: six dimensions read kappa at or below zero on 78 portraits and between 0.43 and 0.66 on 196, and every one has chance agreement above 85 percent. Those carry estimate_is_fragile and should be read as a band, not a number.
Notable-people corpora skew older and are not a population sample.
A dimension can be perfectly reproducible and still not measure what its name claims.

dimensions.scale_citation: Sturm RA, Larsson M (2009). Genetics of human iris colour and patterns. Pigment Cell & Melanoma Research, 22(5). Categorical descriptors aligned with the OCA2/HERC2 phenotype literature.
dimensions.description: Predominant color of the iris. Heterochromia is captured as its own value; mixed colors (e.g. hazel, blue-green) get distinct buckets.

values.definition: Iris appears nearly black under typical lighting; high melanin content. Common in East Asian, South Asian, Sub-Saharan African, and indigenous populations.
Medium to dark brown iris; visible iris detail.
Lighter brown with visible warmth; sometimes called amber when more golden.
Golden-yellow to copper iris; relatively rare. Distinct from light brown by the warmth of the hue.
Mixed brown and green/gold; central iris differs in color from peripheral iris (central heterochromia).
True green; uncommon globally, concentrated in Northern and Eastern European populations.
Mixed blue and green with neither dominant.
True blue; highest frequency in Northern European populations, decreases southward.
Gray to gray-blue iris; lower stromal melanin than blue.
Rare; very low melanin with red light scattering combined with blue stroma.
Two different iris colors — either between eyes (heterochromia iridis) or within one iris (sectoral heterochromia).
Lighting, image quality, or angle prevents reliable iris-color assessment.

observability.notes: Eye color is sensitive to lighting — flash photography and bright daylight can wash out lighter colors; low-light photography can darken lighter eyes toward gray or hazel. Confidence should reflect lighting quality.

dimensions.scale_citation: Aligned with oculoplastic-surgery descriptors and aesthetic-anatomy literature (McCord CD Jr, Codner MA — Eyelid and Periorbital Surgery, 2nd Edition, 2016).
dimensions.description: Overall shape of the visible eye, considering the silhouette of the upper and lower lid margins together. Independent dimension from eyelid_crease_type and epicanthic_fold, which capture finer morphological variation.

values.definition: Slightly elongated horizontal axis; mild taper at lateral and medial canthi. Considered the aesthetic reference shape.
Vertical and horizontal axes approximately equal; minimal canthal taper. Visible sclera above and below the iris.
Upper lid skin descends over the lid crease, partially or fully covering the upper lid platform. Often associated with periorbital aging but can be constitutional.
Smooth upper lid with no visible supratarsal crease. Common in East Asian populations; associated with single eyelid morphology.
Eye sits deep within the orbital socket; pronounced shadow above the upper lid. Brow ridge typically prominent.
Eye sits forward of the orbital socket; sclera visible around the entire iris circumference. Constitutional or proptotic.
Lateral canthus sits below the medial canthus; outer corner droops downward.
Lateral canthus sits above the medial canthus; outer corner angles upward. Common in East Asian populations and as an aging-related lid laxity sign.
Notable left-right shape difference as the dominant feature.

dimensions.scale_citation: McCurdy JA Jr (2005). Cosmetic surgery of the Asian face. Thieme. Chen WP (2007). Asian Blepharoplasty and the Eyelid Crease. Butterworth-Heinemann.
dimensions.description: Morphology of the upper eyelid supratarsal crease. The single most ethnically-variant periocular dimension. The Asian-ophthalmology / Asian-blepharoplasty literature provides the canonical classification system, distinguishing several functional and aesthetic patterns.

values.definition: No visible supratarsal crease; smooth upper lid skin. Approximately 50% of East Asian populations.
Crease present but sits low on the lid, close to the lash line. Common in East Asian populations with double lids.
Mid-position crease; common reference range for European-population eyelids.
High crease position; substantial visible upper lid platform between lash line and crease.
Crease present medially but fades or disappears laterally — or vice versa.
Two or more visible creases on the same lid; commonly age-related but can be constitutional.
One eye is single and the other double — common variation, particularly in East Asian populations.

observability.notes: Best assessed when subject is looking straight ahead with relaxed brow; raised brow can artificially expose creases that aren't typically visible.

dimensions.scale_citation: Duke-Elder S (1964). System of Ophthalmology, Volume III. CV Mosby. The classical four-type Duke-Elder classification (tarsalis, palpebralis, supraciliaris, inversus) remains the standard ophthalmologic vocabulary.
dimensions.description: Presence and morphology of the epicanthic fold — the skin fold of the upper eyelid that may cover the medial canthus. Significant ethnic variation; high prevalence in East Asian, Central Asian, and indigenous American populations.

values.definition: No epicanthic fold; medial canthus clearly visible.
Fold begins at the upper lid skin and inserts on the lower lid, covering the medial canthus. The most common epicanthic-fold variant in East Asian populations.
Fold extends from the upper to the lower lid, covering the medial canthus more symmetrically.
Fold originates at the eyebrow region and continues down to the lacrimal region. Less common; more characteristic of some Inuit and indigenous American populations.
Fold begins at the lower lid and extends upward; partial coverage of the medial canthus from below. Often associated with telecanthus / blepharophimosis syndrome.
Subtle fold residue; medial canthus partially obscured but not fully covered. Can be developmental remnant or post-blepharoplasty result.

dimensions.scale_citation: Farkas LG (1994). Anthropometry of the Head and Face, 2nd Edition. Reference: palpebral fissure axis approximately 10° upslant from horizontal in the European-population aesthetic norm.
dimensions.description: Angle of the palpebral fissure axis (line from medial to lateral canthus) relative to horizontal. Significant ethnic variation; East Asian populations average steeper upslant than European populations.

values.definition: Lateral canthus at the same level as medial canthus; axis approximately 0°.
Lateral canthus slightly higher than medial; ~5-10° above horizontal. Within the European aesthetic reference range.
Lateral canthus substantially higher than medial; >10° above horizontal. Common in East Asian populations.
Lateral canthus slightly below medial; visible fatigue or aging appearance.
Lateral canthus substantially below medial. Associated with genetic syndromes or significant lid laxity.

observability.notes: Best assessed from a directly-frontal photograph with neutral head posture; head-tilt artifacts can be misread as slant.

dimensions.scale_citation: Farkas LG (1994). Anthropometry of the Head and Face, 2nd Edition. Reference: en-ex (medial-canthus to lateral-canthus distance) approximately 28-32mm in adult European-population norms.
dimensions.description: Length of the palpebral fissure (medial canthus to lateral canthus), expressed proportionally relative to intercanthal distance.

values.definition: Fissure length less than intercanthal distance; small visible eye.
Fissure length approximately equal to intercanthal distance.
Fissure length greater than intercanthal distance; large visible eye.

reliability.note: Chance agreement is high because one value dominates this corpus, so kappa is computed on a small (1 - pe) denominator and the estimate moves a long way on a few cells. Measured: between a 78-portrait and a 196-portrait read of the same corpus, dimensions in this regime moved by up to 0.68 of a kappa point, in both directions. Read the band, not the digits.

dimensions.scale_citation: Farkas LG (1994). Anthropometry of the Head and Face, 2nd Edition. Reference: en-en (medial-to-medial canthus distance) approximately 30-34mm in adult European-population norms; relative reference is en-en ≈ palpebral fissure length.
dimensions.description: Distance between the medial canthi, expressed proportionally relative to palpebral fissure length. Captures telecanthus (wide-set eyes) at one extreme.

values.definition: Intercanthal distance less than approximately 90% of palpebral fissure length.
Intercanthal distance approximately equal to palpebral fissure length (Farkas European-population norm).
Intercanthal distance substantially greater than palpebral fissure length. Constitutional in some populations; pathologic in genetic syndromes.

reliability.note: Chance agreement is high because one value dominates this corpus, so kappa is computed on a small (1 - pe) denominator and the estimate moves a long way on a few cells. Measured: between a 78-portrait and a 196-portrait read of the same corpus, dimensions in this regime moved by up to 0.68 of a kappa point, in both directions. Read the band, not the digits.

dimensions.scale_citation: Aligned with craniofacial-anthropology descriptors of supraorbital torus development. Sex-correlated (more prominent in adult males) and with population-level variation.
dimensions.description: Prominence of the supraorbital bony ridge above the eyes. Sex-correlated and with population-level variation.

values.definition: No visible bony prominence above the orbital rim; smooth transition between orbit and forehead.
Visible but not pronounced supraorbital ridge.
Strongly visible supraorbital torus; deep-set appearance to the eyes.

observability.notes: Best assessed from lateral or three-quarter view; frontal view alone can underestimate prominence.

dimensions.scale_citation: Aligned with cosmetic-and-dermatology descriptors of brow density; no single canonical scale.
dimensions.description: Density of native eyebrow hair, untreated. Cosmetic shaping (waxing, threading, microblading, tattooing) affects observed density and should reduce confidence.

values.definition: Few visible hairs; gaps within the brow body.
Brow visible but light density throughout.
Average density.
Thick, full brow with little visible skin within the brow body.
Brow extends into bushy or unibrow territory; high terminal-hair count.

observability.notes: Cosmetic shaping confounds native-density assessment. If brow shows clear evidence of grooming, observation should reflect the visible state and confidence should reflect the uncertainty about native density.

dimensions.scale_citation: Cosmetic-industry shape vocabulary aligned with brow-aesthetics literature (Westmore brow-mapping, etc.).
dimensions.description: Overall arch and shape of the eyebrow as visible in the photograph.

values.definition: Minimal arch; nearly horizontal brow line.
Gentle, gradual arch; arch peak in the lateral two-thirds.
Pronounced arch with a clear peak; stronger lateral-tail descent.
Curved brow without a distinct arch peak; smooth crescent shape.
No arch; brow descends laterally toward the temple.
Notable left-right brow shape difference.

observability.notes: Cosmetic shaping affects observation; flag when shaping is visible.

dimensions.scale_citation: Aligned with the Hirmand classification of tear-trough deformity (Hirmand H — Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 2010, 125(2)) for visible severity.
dimensions.description: Visible darkness or hollowness in the infraorbital region (under-eye). Constitutional in some ethnic groups (notably South Asian, Mediterranean populations); also age-related and lifestyle-related.

values.definition: No discernible darkness or hollowness.
Subtle pigmentation or shallow tear-trough; not the dominant feature of the periorbital region.
Clearly visible darkness or hollowness; periorbital region appears tired.
Pronounced infraorbital pigmentation or deep tear-trough; significant aesthetic concern in cosmetic-medicine context.

observability.notes: Lighting affects assessment substantially — overhead lighting can artificially deepen tear-trough shadows.

dimensions.scale_citation: Aligned with ophthalmologic exophthalmometry descriptors (Hertel exophthalmometry); qualitative-bucket equivalent for visual assessment.
dimensions.description: Anteroposterior position of the globe relative to the orbital rim. Constitutional variation; pathologic at the extremes (proptosis / enophthalmos).

values.definition: Globe sits posterior to the orbital rim; deep-set appearance.
Globe at typical orbital rim position.
Globe sits anterior to the orbital rim; visible sclera around the iris circumference.

observability.notes: Best assessed from lateral view. Differential diagnosis between constitutional prominence and pathologic proptosis (e.g. thyroid eye disease) is outside the scope of phenotype observation.

references: Farkas LG (1994). Anthropometry of the Head and Face, 2nd Edition. Raven Press.
Duke-Elder S (1964). System of Ophthalmology, Volume III. CV Mosby.
Sturm RA, Larsson M (2009). Genetics of human iris colour and patterns. Pigment Cell & Melanoma Research, 22(5).
McCurdy JA Jr (2005). Cosmetic surgery of the Asian face. Thieme.
Chen WP (2007). Asian Blepharoplasty and the Eyelid Crease. Butterworth-Heinemann.
McCord CD Jr, Codner MA (2016). Eyelid and Periorbital Surgery, 2nd Edition. Quality Medical Publishing.
Hirmand H (2010). Anatomy and nonsurgical correction of the tear trough deformity. Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 125(2).
Putterman AM (1999). Cosmetic Oculoplastic Surgery, 3rd Edition. WB Saunders.
